routes.description: Establish that early Christian sources report a transformed but physically continuous risen Jesus and that their cumulative historical provenance supports occurrence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony is historically usable, bodily in meaning, and better explained by Jesus having physically risen than by the proposed alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically grounded early testimony about Jesus after death to the conclusion that the body that died was raised in transformed physical continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and other early Christian testimony preserves resurrection claims sufficiently early and coherently to bear historical weight.
Show that spiritual and glorious body language denotes transformed embodiment rather than an immaterial survival or apparition.
Connect reported appearances and geographically dispersed early teaching to identifiable witnesses or apostolic transmission.
Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan analogues and account for costly early proclamation without dissolving it into ordinary legend.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use costly adherence and continued proclamation to support the sincerity and claimed eyewitness grounding of the resurrection belief.
Treat convergence among distinct early sources and communities as support for a common antecedent resurrection tradition.

routes.description: Withhold the bodily-resurrection conclusion by applying ordinary historical analogy and challenging the meaning, provenance, and independence of the Christian testimony.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources do not historically distinguish a bodily resurrection from spiritual interpretation, legendary transmission, inherited ideology, or comparable religious narratives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant inferring an actual bodily return from death under provisional, analogy-based historical inquiry.

centralBridges.description: Apply comparison with ordinary experience and ancient religious narratives when judging the probability of an extraordinary resurrection report.
Show that Pauline flesh, spirit, and spiritual-body language does not require physical continuity with Jesus's dead body.
Challenge the authorship, consistency, independence, and apostolic pedigree of the documents and transmission chains offered as evidence.
Provide nonmiraculous explanations for uniform belief, costly commitment, martyrdom traditions, and the movement's expansion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between divine ability to resurrect and historical evidence that a resurrection actually occurred.
Identify pre-Christian or ancient structural parallels that weaken an inference from narrative uniqueness to historical occurrence.

sectionSelections.title: Historical method and extraordinary-event inference
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion requires an inference from ancient reports to an extraordinary event, making the governing historical standard and the evidential role of early reports foundational to both routes.

proSelections.proposition: Paul's received tradition in First Corinthians 15 preserves an early proclamation that Christ died, was buried, rose, and appeared to named groups and individuals.
Paul and several Gospel accounts report overlapping appearances to Peter, women, disciples, and others, supplying multiple attestation for postmortem encounters.

conSelections.proposition: Historical conclusions must remain inductive and provisional, while prior religious commitment can cause apologetic reasoning to defend a conclusion adopted on other grounds.
Because credible present experience supplies no comparable resurrections while ancient religion supplies many extraordinary narratives, analogy makes myth more probable than bodily return from death.

sectionSelections.title: Meaning of bodily and spiritual resurrection language
sectionSelections.rationale: Whether the earliest resurrection language describes transformed physical continuity or an immaterial spiritual condition bears directly on the bodily qualification in the motion.

proSelections.proposition: Paul describes Christ's glorious body as the model for the transformation of believers' lowly bodies, indicating resurrected embodiment rather than immaterial survival.
Paul contrasts mortal corruption with a glorified incorruptible body, and his usage of spiritual denotes Spirit-transformed embodiment rather than an immaterial entity.

conSelections.proposition: First Corinthians 15 says flesh and blood cannot inherit God's kingdom and contrasts a natural body with a spiritual one, creating tension with Luke's flesh-and-bones depiction.
The immediate First Corinthians context contrasts mortal flesh with spirit, so broader lexical usage does not establish continuity with a tangible physical body.

sectionSelections.title: Provenance and coherence of Pauline testimony
sectionSelections.rationale: Pauline material is among the earliest evidence invoked, so whether its received and revealed formulations are coherent materially affects the historical foundation of the resurrection claim.

proSelections.proposition: Paul can consistently describe the resurrection proclamation as delivered to him and as received from Christ, as First Corinthians 11 and Galatians both permit direct revelation.

conSelections.proposition: First Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1 appear to conflict over whether Paul received the gospel from human transmitters or directly from the Lord, raising doubts about coherence or authorship.

sectionSelections.title: Chronology and relevance of pagan resurrection analogues
sectionSelections.rationale: The presence or absence of earlier comparable dying-and-rising traditions affects whether the Christian accounts are treated as historically distinctive testimony or as familiar religious narrative forms.

proSelections.proposition: The earliest evidence for Attis contains no resurrection account, while written resurrection interpretations appear only later in the Christian era.
Justin Martyr presents pagan stories as imitations, affirms Christ's priority and distinctive ending, and therefore does not establish a pre-Christian resurrection parallel.

conSelections.proposition: Osiris is restored from death, acts afterward, and rules the netherworld, creating a structural analogue to Jesus's resurrection and ascent.
Ugaritic evidence supports Baal's death and return, while early Christian counterfeit explanations presuppose pagan parallels that Christians believed required explanation.

sectionSelections.title: Independence and reliability of apostolic transmission
sectionSelections.rationale: The historical force of later Christian agreement depends on whether it preserves independently grounded apostolic information or merely repeats contested attributions and normative inherited teaching.

proSelections.proposition: Early writers including Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, and Irenaeus teach fleshly resurrection within claimed lines of instruction connecting them to apostles and eyewitnesses.
Agreement among geographically and culturally separated early Christian writers is explained by traditions traceable to apostles, including their shared bodily-resurrection belief.

conSelections.proposition: The resurrection case assumes disputed authorship and authenticity across anonymous or uncertain New Testament and patristic writings, treating later church tradition as historical identification.
Apostolic pedigree does not establish reliable transmission because rival teachers made analogous succession claims and falsely attributed writings were widespread.

sectionSelections.title: Martyrdom, costly commitment, and movement growth
sectionSelections.rationale: Claims about suffering and expansion can support the sincerity or origins of resurrection belief only if their historical basis and explanatory connection to the event are established.

proSelections.proposition: Costly conversions and sustained proclamation under persecution are best explained by contact with eyewitness testimony that Jesus was physically alive after death.

conSelections.proposition: Apostolic identities, activities, and martyrdoms are too poorly documented and dependent on late legendary narratives to support an inference to resurrection.
Martyrdom demonstrates sincerity rather than truth, while social service, demographic practices, accessibility, and ordinary conversion dynamics can explain Christianity's growth.
